newsitem.title: CANADA: TransCanada reveals major expansion plans.
newsitem.headline: TransCanada reveals major expansion plans.

text.p: TransCanada PipeLines Ltd on Tuesday fired its long-awaited salvo in Canada's natural gas pipeline expansion battle, revealing it could add 2.3 billion cubic feet of transport capacity by the turn of the century at a cost of C$2.6 billion.
If TransCanada's projections come to pass, its pipeline system, now the main route to eastern markets for Alberta gas, would have a capacity approaching 10 billion cubic feet a day.
"It is the largest single expansion of the TransCanada system ever anticipated," TransCanada Vice-President Bob Reid told reporters.
The Canadian mainline has a current capacity of about 7.2 billion cubic feet a day.

The company, which filed the first phase of its "Nexus" expansion program with Canada's National Energy Board on Tuesday, said it applied to add 465 million cubic feet of capacity on its Canadian mainline in 1998 at a cost of C$1.1 billion.
But TransCanada said it had firm commitments from gas producers, local distribution companies and marketers totalling 1.25 billion cubic feet a day.

The remaining 785 million cubic feet a day would be part of a phase II application to be filed later this year, Reid said. Company officials also said they expected more agreements to flow in from prospective customers above that volume.

The second phase would be centered on the expansion of TransCanada's affiliated Great Lakes Gas Transmission system in the northern United States which, if approved by the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, would be in service by 1999.

The expansion would add a high-pressure third line along the Great Lakes right-of-way to Sarnia, Ontario from Emerson Manitoba via Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan to feed numerous downstream pipeline proposals in the United States announced over the past few months.
"The long-term economics show that it is better to use the Great Lakes Route because the capital costs are lower," Reid said.

TransCanada is locked in a battle to expand takeaway capacity for Alberta natural gas with Alliance Pipeline, a C$3.6 billion producer-backed proposal to ship gas directly to Chicago from northeastern British Columbia.
Partners in Alliance, which would have a capacity of 1.3 billion cubic feet a day, include such companies as Alberta Energy Co Ltd, Gulf Canada Resources Ltd and IPL Energy Inc -- 18 in all.

Reid stressed the Nexus expansion was not a response to Alliance, but to market demand in the key U.S. Midwest, Northeast and eastern Canadian regions, where numerous pipeline links from TransCanada's system are proposed.
But the competitive nature of the projects -- which would both offer major new capacity to Chicago -- reared its head several times during a media briefing.
Reid said Nexus would be superior to Alliance because it could add capacity in stages, as opposed to in one fell swoop, which would mean plans could change with market conditions.

He also said rolled-in tolls on the expanded system, which would likely be 1.2 cents (Canadian) per gigajoule higher than under the current rate in the Eastern Zone, would be favorable for shippers. "We will be competitive -- nose to nose with Alliance -- I can guarantee that."
Alliance plans are before the U.S. FERC and the partners plan to file their full application with Canada's NEB soon.
TransCanada is already adding 300 million cubic feet a day of capacity for November 1997.
